title: 4 Easy Guidelines To Calling On Students While Eliminating Rudeness, Disruptions, And Calling Out
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents four guidelines for how teachers should respond to raised hands to eliminate disruptive, attention-grabbing behavior while keeping participation fair and low-stress. The steps are to wait before selecting a student, make brief eye contact with volunteers so they know they've been seen, call on only students demonstrating proper hand-raising, and address call-outs as rule-breaking disruptions handled calmly after the discussion moves on. He argues these small behavioral shifts by the teacher—not new rules for students—are what actually make participation feel safe and equitable. The piece frames this as part of a broader principle that a teacher's own actions drive classroom outcomes more than what is said.
points: Pausing before calling on anyone gives every student time to think and removes the pressure to blurt out answers immediately.
Making brief eye contact with volunteers reassures students they've been seen, even if they aren't chosen to answer.
Only calling on students following proper hand-raising etiquette eliminates aggressive hand-waving and groaning.
Call-outs should be treated as rule-breaking disruptions, but the consequence should be delivered later, after the discussion moves on, not immediately.
It is the teacher's behavior in response to hand-raising, more than the rules taught about it, that determines whether participation feels safe and fair.
quotes: The way you call on your students when they raise their hand can have a strong impact on learning and behavior.
Waiting also lowers the stress in the room. It does away with the notion that your students must compete to be heard.
They need to know that you see them and that you’re not making your decision based on who is closest, most aggressive, or within your immediate field of vision.
So unless they’re quiet and sitting down in their seats with their hand straight up in the air, you will not call upon them—ever, ever, ever.
Waiting until the moment passes before enforcing a consequence protects the flow of discussion and enables you to handle the situation gracefully and without confrontation.
